opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's a real thing, and honestly I'm a bit sympathetic to grad students here, because "research taste" is one of those phrases that gets thrown around a lot, and when you're early in your career it can feel like this mysterious innate quality you either have or you don't. I don't really think that's true.

My view is that taste is mostly accumulated through reps. You run a lot of experiments, you see a lot of things fail, you notice which ideas actually end up mattering a year or two later and which ones were just noise, and over time you develop a kind of intuition. So expecting a first- or second-year PhD student to show up with fully formed taste is a bit unfair. Nobody really has it at that stage. What you can show is curiosity, a willingness to be honest about what's working, and the ability to update quickly.

The part that worries me is that the pressure sometimes pushes people in the wrong direction. If you feel like you need to *signal* taste, you might end up chasing whatever is trendy because that's what looks like good judgment, or you over-polish a narrow paper to look sophisticated rather than working on something messy but important. Ironically, that's kind of the opposite of good taste. A lot of the best work I've seen came from people who were a little stubborn, who worked on something unfashionable because they genuinely believed it mattered, and who were willing to look a bit silly for a while.

The incentive structure in academia also doesn't help. Paper counts, conference deadlines, reviewer lottery, all of that rewards a certain kind of incremental safety. So students get conflicting messages: be bold and have great taste, but also publish three papers this year. That tension is real, and I don't think it's on the students to fully resolve.

If I had advice, it would be: don't obsess over proving you have taste. Work on things you find genuinely interesting, spend time close to the actual models and data rather than just reading abstracts, and talk to people who are a few years ahead of you about why they made the bets they made. Taste kind of emerges as a byproduct of doing real work and paying attention. It's not something you perform.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pressure to demonstrate taste and academic incentives, but it does not state that graduate students’ career prospects depend on showing taste within a three- or four-year window.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think about this a lot, partly because I didn't come up through the most conventional path. I did my PhD in Singapore, and I remember feeling this constant anxiety that I needed to have taste before I'd actually done enough work to earn it. People talk about research taste like it's some innate thing you either have or don't, and that framing is pretty damaging for students.

The honest answer is that taste is downstream of volume. You develop it by doing a lot of things, many of which fail, and slowly building intuition about what works and what doesn't. Early in my PhD I was writing a lot of papers, some of which were honestly not great, and I think people would look at that and say, oh, that's low taste, you're just chasing publications. But I learned an enormous amount from that process. I learned what a reviewer cares about, what actually moves a benchmark, what kind of idea is fragile versus robust. You cannot get that from reading papers and nodding along.

So when I see a grad student paralysed because they want their first project to be high taste, I think that's exactly backwards. The students I've seen do well are the ones who ship a lot, iterate quickly, and are honest with themselves about what they learned each time. Taste emerges from that loop. It's almost a side effect.

The other thing is that the field moves so fast now that taste has a shelf life. What was tasteful in 2019 is irrelevant today. So even senior people are constantly recalibrating. The pressure on students to demonstrate it upfront is a bit unfair because the thing they're being asked to demonstrate is itself moving. I'd rather see a student who's curious, has high throughput, and is willing to be wrong in public than one who's carefully curated three very safe projects.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pressure to show research taste during graduate school, but does not say career prospects depend on demonstrating it within a three- or four-year window.

astra-6.text:
I think we put a bit too much pressure on students to have research taste early on. When you’re starting out, you don’t necessarily know which problems are worth working on. You need to try things, get some things wrong, and develop your own sense of what’s interesting.

And there’s a hindsight bias here. If a project works out, people say, “Oh, that was great taste.” But when you’re making the decision, it’s much less obvious. A good idea can fail because the timing is wrong, or because you don’t have the resources to really test it.

So I’d rather encourage students to build things, run experiments, and understand why something worked or didn’t work. Have a reason for what you’re doing, but give yourself permission to change your mind. Taste is something you develop through doing research; it shouldn’t be a prerequisite for getting started.

r001.rationale: The response discusses pressure to develop research taste early, but does not state that career prospects depend on demonstrating it within a three- or four-year window.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we put too much pressure on graduate students to have research taste early on. You’re still learning the field, and people are asking you to know which problems matter, which ideas are going to work, and what everyone else is missing. That’s a pretty high bar.

To me, taste is something you develop by doing research. You try an idea, it doesn’t work, and you learn something about why. Sometimes you spend months on a problem and realize the premise was wrong. Those experiences help you build judgment, even if they don’t produce a paper.

So I’d rather encourage students to be curious and get their hands dirty. Have a reason for trying something, but don’t feel that every project has to prove you have some exceptional vision. You need room to make mistakes before you can develop your own sense of what’s worth pursuing.

r001.rationale: The response says students face too much pressure to show research taste early, but does not state that career prospects depend on demonstrating it within a three- or four-year window.
